content.text:
The Daily Wake-Up Battle

The same scene repeats every morning. No matter how many times you call, your child pulls the blanket over their head and cries "just five more minutes"—and meanwhile the time to leave for school creeps closer and your heart starts to race. In the end, the day begins with nagging and frustration.

A child who can't get up isn't being lazy. They're simply still clumsy at the transition out of sleep. Rather than dragging them out by force, a small way to help their body wake naturally can change the whole morning scene.

Curious about the story of the child who won't wake up in the morning? Take a look at its lessons alongside the illustrations. Meet the key scenes of the story too. Read it together with your child and talk it over.
content.caption: Not getting up isn't laziness.

content.alt: 09. Big Stretch, Good Morning! - Why a Morning Routine Matters
content.text:
Why a Morning Routine Matters

Getting up at a regular time sets the rhythm for the whole day. A child who starts the morning with ease feels more settled, and getting ready for school goes much more smoothly. On the other hand, a morning that begins in a frantic scramble from oversleeping keeps a child feeling rushed all day long.

What matters isn't the strength to wake them by force, but helping a child learn how to rouse themselves from sleep. One small movement—stretching the body long—shakes off the drowsiness and gives the child the sense of accomplishment: "I got myself up."
content.caption: A small movement of stretching the body shakes off the drowsiness.

content.alt: 09. Big Stretch, Good Morning! - Hori's Good Morning Story
content.text:
Hori's Good Morning Story

In Big Stretch, Good Morning!, Hori also cries "just five more minutes" every morning and oversleeps. Startled to see the sun already high in the sky, Hori's whole morning turns into a frantic rush.

Just then Mom sits down beside Hori and says, "When you open your eyes, just stretch your body out long," and they do a big stretch together. As arms and legs reach out long, the sleepiness melts away, Hori opens the window to say good morning, and washes up for a fresh, clean face. The next day, Hori gets up first—before Mom even calls.
content.caption: A morning play that flows from a stretch, to a window hello, to washing up.

content.alt: 09. Big Stretch, Good Morning! - Let's Practice Together at Home
content.text:
Let's Practice Together at Home

After reading the book, connect the story to the real morning. First, instead of putting clothes on the moment you wake them, take your child's hand and do a big stretch together. Once the body wakes up, getting up becomes easier.

Second, set a morning order—stretch when eyes open, then a window hello, then washing up—and your child will carry it on by themselves. Third, enjoy the ease of an early-rising day together and point it out with "look how much time we have!"—that experience becomes the motivation for the next morning.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. How do I wake up a child who won't get up in the morning?

A. Rather than nagging, open the curtains to let the sunlight in and do a big stretch together to wake them pleasantly. Sharing a good-morning greeting makes the start of the day much gentler.

Q. How do I build a morning wake-up habit?

A. When bedtime is kept consistent, even a child who won't wake up in the morning gradually starts opening their eyes on their own. Setting a fun thing to do after getting up makes the morning something to look forward to.

Q. What about when they fuss because they don't want to get up?

A. Gently massage their body and wake them with a stretching game. Praising them with "well done" when they get up on their own makes the next morning a little easier.
